definition.synopsis: This course teaches students to turn data into charts that answer a stated question for a stated audience. Students learn to abstract data and tasks, to choose marks and channels that suit human perception, and to use colour, layout and interaction with accessibility in mind. They build charts for categorical, temporal, geospatial, network and hierarchical data with a reproducible tool chain, critique published visualisations for the ways they mislead, and evaluate competing designs with evidence from a usability check. Uncertainty and the ethics of representation run through every topic. In a team project, students carry a dataset from cleaning to a data story for a stakeholder audience, and each student defends the team's design choices in an individual defence. The course is assessed by labs, quizzes, a critique essay, the project and a final examination.

assessment.title: Individual project defence
assessment.description: Each student defends the team's design choices in a 10 to 15 minute conversation, with evidence from the team's usability check, so each student's evidence for CLO4 is their own. Marked against the defence rubric.

assessment.description: A 1,500-word critique of a published visualisation that locates where and why it misleads, against perception, Gestalt, accessibility and ethics criteria.

assessment.description: A three-hour written examination in three sections. Section A, short answers on abstraction, marks, channels and perception (CLO1, 12 marks). The marking scheme awards marks for the reasoning stated, not for the chart alone: in Section C, 6 marks for the criteria named, 6 for weighing the designs against them and 4 for a recommendation that follows from the weighing.

slides.title: Three questions before any chart
bullets: What: what kind of data is in front of us?
Why: what is the reader trying to do: look something up, compare, find a trend?
How: which marks and channels will carry it?
slides.notes: This is the what, why and how framework from Munzner 2014, and the whole course hangs on it. Stress that the why comes before the how.

slides.title: What a good chart gets right
bullets: It answers the question it was made for

bullets: Starting from the tool's default chart

# Lab sheet 1: the tool chain and a first chart

Sample, synthetic: written for this prototype. Week 1, not marked.

## Goal

Install the course tool chain and reproduce one chart from a supplied notebook, so every later lab starts from a working setup.

## Steps

1. Install the tool chain listed on the course page, in the order given there.
2. Open the week 1 notebook and run it from the top. Every cell should finish without an error.
3. Reproduce the bar chart of the supplied sales table.
4. Change one encoding, the colour or the order of the bars, and note what changed for a reader.
5. Under the chart, write the question it answers in one sentence.

## Check before you leave

Show a demonstrator your running notebook and your sentence.

## If you are stuck

The course page lists the known installation problems and their fixes. Ask the person next to you before you ask a demonstrator.

slides.title: Time has a direction
bullets: Time is ordered, so readers expect earlier on the left and later on the right
Most questions about time are about change: a trend, a season, a break
Today: lines, seasonality and small multiples
slides.notes: Start with a monthly series on the screen and ask what changed. Collect three different answers; each is a different question.

slides.title: Line or bar?
bullets: A line for continuous change across many points
Bars for counts in a few separate periods
Never join points that are not a sequence
slides.notes: The classic error is a line through categories. Show it once, then never again.

slides.title: Seeing the season
bullets: A yearly cycle can hide the trend beneath it
Plot each month across the years to see the season
Or take the season out and show what is left

figure.label: Figure: a monthly series with its yearly cycle marked, drawn in the lab from this week's dataset

slides.notes: Do the seasonal plot live if the projector allows; otherwise describe it and let the lab show it.

slides.title: Small multiples
bullets: One small chart per category, all on the same scale
The eye compares shapes across the panels
Shared axes keep the comparison honest
slides.notes: Tufte's term. The key decision is the shared scale; free scales make every panel look equally dramatic.

slides.title: Two y-axes, one trap
bullets: Two scales chosen freely
Any crossing point can be manufactured
Readers compare heights that mean nothing
right: Or two panels on one time axis
Say the units in the title
slides.notes: Ask a volunteer to move one axis and make the lines cross. The room will see why the chart proves nothing.

slides.title: Annotate the change
bullets: Mark the event that explains a break
Put the label on the line, not in a legend
One annotation the reader needs beats five they do not
slides.notes: This is the habit the project report is marked on under clarity: the reader should not have to guess why the line moved.

## Data

The week 6 dataset on the course page: a synthetic monthly series for six regions over three years.

2. Facet the same data into small multiples, one panel a region, all on one shared scale.

4. Title the figure with its finding, not its axes.
5. In two sentences, say why the shared scale matters here.

The notebook, by the end of week 6. It must rebuild the figure from the raw file.

The shared scale, the annotation, the finding title and a notebook that runs from the top.

Sample, synthetic: written for this prototype. Week 7, not marked: practice for the critique essay due in week 9.

## In pairs

You have three published charts on the workshop sheet. For each one, answer:

# The project brief

Sample, synthetic: written for this prototype. Released in week 8.

## The task

In teams of three, take a public dataset from raw file to a written data story for a stakeholder you name. The story must answer the stakeholder's question and end in actions they could take.

## What you hand in

1. A packaged workbook that rebuilds every chart from the raw data with documented steps.
2. A written report of at most six pages: the stakeholder and their question; the dataset and how you cleaned it; the descriptive figures; the core charts, with at least one map; the story; and the actions you recommend.
3. A usability check of your main chart with at least three readers outside your team: what they misread, and what you changed.

## The defence

Each student defends the team's design choices in a 10 to 15 minute conversation in week 14, using the evidence from the usability check. The defence is marked for each student on their own.

## Dates

Brief in week 8; draft to the studio critique in week 13; report at the end of week 13; defences in week 14.

## Marking

Team report, 15% of the course, on the project rubric: design and accessibility (3), reproducibility of the pipeline (2), clarity and integrity of the communication (5), insight for the audience (5). Individual defence, 10%, on the defence rubric.

## Integrity

Cite every dataset and every source on the chart it supports. A chart you cannot rebuild from the workbook is not yet part of the report.

CS310.synopsis: This course teaches students to turn data into charts that answer a stated question for a stated audience. Students learn to abstract data and tasks, to choose marks and channels that suit human perception, and to use colour, layout and interaction with accessibility in mind. They build charts for categorical, temporal, geospatial, network and hierarchical data with a reproducible tool chain, critique published visualisations for the ways they mislead, and evaluate competing designs with evidence from a usability check. Uncertainty and the ethics of representation run through every topic. In a team project, students carry a dataset from cleaning to a data story for a stakeholder audience, and each student defends the team's design choices in an individual defence. The course is assessed by labs, quizzes, a critique essay, the project and a final examination.

criteria.name: Design and accessibility
levels: Every chart fits its data and task; colour, contrast and labels pass the accessibility checklist without exception.
Charts fit their data and task, with one or two minor accessibility lapses.

Chart choices are unexplained or misleading, and accessibility is not considered.

criteria.name: Reproducibility of the pipeline
levels: The packaged workbook rebuilds every chart from the raw data with one documented command.
The workbook rebuilds the charts with a few documented manual steps.
Some charts cannot be rebuilt from the workbook as supplied.
The charts cannot be traced back to the data.

criteria.name: Clarity and integrity of the communication, sources cited
levels: The story answers the stated question in order; every figure is sourced and no chart distorts its data.
The story is clear and sourced, with one weak transition or one unsourced figure.
The story wanders or leaves figures unsourced, and one chart distorts its data.
There is no clear story, sources are missing and several charts distort their data.

criteria.name: Insight for the audience
levels: Findings are specific to the named stakeholder and end in a recommendation the stakeholder can act on.
Findings suit the stakeholder; the recommendation is general.
Findings are stated but not tied to the stakeholder's decision.
Charts are shown without findings.

criteria.name: Evaluation of the competing designs
levels: Compares at least two designs against the stakeholder's question and defends the choice with evidence.
Compares two designs and defends the choice, with evidence for most claims.
Describes the designs but defends the choice by preference.
Cannot say why the team's design was chosen.

criteria.name: Use of the usability check's evidence
levels: Uses the usability check's findings, the inconvenient ones included, to justify a change.
Uses the findings to justify the design, leaving out one inconvenient result.
Mentions the usability check without drawing on its findings.
Uses no usability evidence.

assessment.description: A 1,500-word critique of a published visualisation that locates where and why it misleads, against perception, Gestalt, accessibility and ethics criteria.

assessment.title: Final examination
assessment.description: A three-hour written examination in three sections. Section A, short answers on abstraction, marks, channels and perception (CLO1, 12 marks). Section B, construct and annotate charts from a supplied table (CLO2, 12 marks). Section C, evaluate two competing designs for a stated question (CLO4, 16 marks). The marking scheme awards marks for the reasoning stated, not for the chart alone: in Section C, 6 marks for the criteria named, 6 for weighing the designs against them and 4 for a recommendation that follows from the weighing.
